question: Robert Ray Redfield Jr., former head of the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), was responsible for their management during the COVID-19 pandemic. After initial analyses, Redfield concluded in 2021 that SARS-CoV-2 was likely to have originated from a laboratory in Wuhan (lab-leak hypothesis) and not from natural transmission from animals to humans1.

2 He stressed that the virus was transmitted unusually efficiently from person to person, making natural formation unlikely. Redfield particularly criticised gain-of-function research on high-risk viruses, funded by, among others, the National Institutes of Health (NIH), the US State Department, the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) and the US Department of Defence3.

He said that such research had so far not prevented any pandemic, but may instead have contributed to the biggest pandemic in modern history. Following his hearing, the US House of Representatives unanimously voted in favour of a draft law requiring intelligence services to disclose information on the origin of SARSCoV-24. 1.
Where in the EU is gain-of-function research carried out and what exactly is being researched there?
Is it ethically justifiable to manipulate viruses with pandemic potential if the benefits are scientifically unproven?
What is the Commission’s view of the origin of the COVID-19 virus and what scientific evidence is this view based on?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (8.4.2026) With regard to gain-of-function research, the Commission refers the Honourable Member to the answers to Parliamentary Questions E-002369/20251 and E-004131/20252, detailing the Commission's risk management measures, eligibility criteria, ethical considerations and security checks to support gain-of-function research on respiratory diseases.

It is imperative that all research activities rigorously adhere to established scientific methods, demonstrate measurable scientific excellence, and operate within the bounds of the applicable legal frameworks, including strict compliance with norms, safety regulations, and security standards, particularly when research involves the handling or manipulation of pathogenic viruses.

Beyond ensuring compliance with relevant national, EU, and international legislation, research activities funded through Horizon Europe must also strictly follow the principles of research ethics and integrity3. Any research activity that presents disproportionate or unmitigated risks to human health, the environment, or society at large is deemed ineligible for funding.
This ensures that Horizon Europe upholds the highest standards of responsibility, safety, and societal accountability.

With regard to the origin of the COVID-19, the Commission refers the Honourable Member to the answers to Parliamentary Questions E-003628/20254, E-002534/20255, E-001403/20256 and E-001040/20257, detailing when and from what source EU institutions became aware of a possible upcoming COVID-19 pandemic and the Commission’s view of the origin of the SARS-CoV2 virus.

1 https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/E-10-2025-002369-ASW_EN.html. 2 https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/E-10-2025-004131-ASW_EN.html. 3 As spelled out in Article 19 of the Horizon Europe Regulation: ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2021/695/oj. 4 https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/E-10-2025-003628-ASW_EN.html. 5 https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/P-10-2025-002534-ASW_EN.
